list.listitem: Diagnosis in both adults and children is typically clinical, with a classic presentation of right lower quadrant abdominal pain followed by nausea and vomiting, low-grade fever, positive psoas sign, tachycardia, and guarding. Use of a decision tool can assist in determining the probability of appendicitis. C

For patients with atypical presentation or intermediate probability of appendicitis, CT, ultrasound or MRI should be considered. Scoring systems combined with lab and imaging yield the highest accuracy. B

Once the diagnosis of appendicitis is entertained, an early surgical consult is recommended. In addition, patients should refrain from eating or drinking and be started on intravenous fluids and antibiotics. A If necessary, refer to a center with appropriate resources to care for potentially very ill children. A

For patients with acute uncomplicated appendicitis, nonoperative treatment with antibiotics should be considered and is successful in 62% to 73% of patients. A For patients with complicated appendicitis, including pregnant patients, operative management is likely preferred over non-operative management. B
Data are conflicting with respect to use of laparoscopic approaches vs. open appendectomy; clinical outcomes are usually similar, especially for complicated appendicitis and for children. B

background.definition: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, a hollow muscular tube arising from the cecum in proximity to the ileocecal valve.

list.listitem: The rate of acute appendicitis in the US has increased from 0.76 per 1000 to 0.94 per 1000 between 1993 and 2008. The highest frequency was found in the 10- to 19-year-old age group. Rates remained higher in men. Hispanics, Asians, and Native Americans, while frequencies decreased among whites and blacks.
Seven percent of the population develops appendicitis in their lifetime (8.6% of boys/men, 6.7% girls/women).
In a UK review of 14 studies, primary care mean consultation prevalence for abdominal pain was 2.8%, with appendicitis diagnosed in 1.9% of cases.
Appendicitis surgery is the most common abdominal surgical emergency.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 27 studies including 25,547 patients undergoing laparoscopy for suspected acute appendicitis found a rate of unexpected pathology of 3.5% (95% CI 2.7-4.3%; moderate certainty). Appendiceal malignancy was identified in 1.0% (95% CI 0.8-1.3%; high certainty); other findings were benign appendiceal pathology and gynecologic and gastrointestinal pathology.
Acute obstruction of the appendiceal lumen from appendicolith (fecalith) or extrinsic obstruction lymphadenopathy.

Obstruction from tumor, parasite, or foreign body—in a case series of 141 patients, 10 (7.1%) were diagnosed with neoplasia including 4 with colonic adenocarcinoma, 3 with mucinous tumors, and 1 with a carcinoid tumor.
Rarely, following trauma.

Inflammation of the appendix causes an increase in intraluminal pressure and is transmitted through afferent sympathetic and vagal fibers that conduct visceral pain referred initially to the periumbilical region.
Persistent inflammation results in peritoneal inflammation and right lower quadrant (RLQ) pain.
Retrocecal position of the appendix delays presentation of peritoneal signs.
With progression of the inflammation, the appendix becomes hypoxic and gangrenous, which can result in serosal perforation.

Diagnosis in both adults and children is typically clinical, with a classic presentation of RLQ abdominal pain followed by nausea and vomiting, low-grade fever, positive psoas sign, tachycardia, and guarding. C

Clinical decision rules such as the Alvarado score and Ohmann score can perform as well as a skilled surgeon in risk stratification.B The newest score, RIPASA, appears to more sensitive than the Alvarado score, particularly in Asian populations. B
The combination of elevated WBC count and elevated CRP levels is strong evidence in favor of appendicitis; the diagnosis is much less likely if both are normal. C

For patients with atypical presentation or intermediate probability of appendicitis, consider computed tomography (CT) with contrast, ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Ultrasound is preferred in children because of the lower radiation exposure and cost. B The American College of Radiology (ACR) recommends either abdominal ultrasound or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast for pregnant women with suspected appendicitis. B

list.listitem: Patients typically present with vague, poorly localized, periumbilical pain and intermittent abdominal cramping. With progression, severe pain localizes to right lower quadrant in approximately two thirds of patients. Patients also typically have low-grade fever and tachycardia.

Anorexia is uncommon in children. Nausea and vomiting usually follows abdominal pain. Pain before vomiting is present in 99% of patients with appendicitis; vomiting before pain makes appendicitis very unlikely. This applies to children, as well as to adults.

A single question about worsening pain elicited when driving over a speed bump can be helpful in ruling out appendicitis (negative predictive value in one study was 90%; 95% CI, 56%-100%). In a small study in which 64/101 patients had traveled over a speed bump, almost all (97%) of the 53 patients with confirmed appendicitis reported worsening pain associated with a speed bump. Of the patients without appendicitis, 70% also reported pain. In a recent prospective study of 100 consecutive adult patients with suspected appendicitis, 77 of the 85 patients diagnosed with appendicitis reported worsened pain over speed bumps. Sensitivity of this sign was 90.5%, specificity was 40%, positive predictive value was 96.25%, negative predictive value was 20%, positive likelihood ratio was 1.5 and negative likelihood ratio was 0.23.
Tachycardia in children that is unresponsive or minimally responsive to fluid challenge suggests appendicitis. Urinary frequency and dysuria may occur when the appendix lies adjacent to the bladder.

Physical findings vary with time and specific location of the appendix. Tenderness to percussion and rebound tenderness are often, but not always, present. Assessing for rebound tenderness in children with appendicitis is often traumatic and does not usually add to the physical examination. By having the patient jump on the right foot or cough, the pain may localize to the RLQ. Pain elicited on hopping or jumping appears to be a reasonably sensitive and specific indicator of appendicitis in children.
McBurney's point tenderness is appendiceal pain located along an imaginary line one third of the distance between the anterior superior iliac spine and the umbilicus.
Rovsing's sign: left-side palpation produces right-side tenderness.

The psoas sign (pain with hip extension) is helpful in both adults and children. It is very specific and helpful when positive but its absence does not significantly reduce the likelihood of appendicitis.
Obturator sign is pain on hip flexion and external rotation.

Diagnosis is typically clinical. Of patients with suspected appendicitis, about one third have confirmed appendicitis. Normal to moderate leukocytosis with neutrophilia is often present, but a normal white blood cell (WBC) count does not rule out appendicitis. Similarly, the CRP level is often elevated but a normal value does not rule out appendicitis. In one meta-analysis, CRP had higher accuracy for acute appendicitis than WBC count or procalcitonin, with an area under the curve of 0.75 (95% CI, 0.71-0.78). An elevated procalcitonin appears useful for ruling in complicated appendicitis.

Authors of a scoping review of biomarkers for acute appendicitis concluded that routine biomarkers (e.g., WBC count and procalcitonin) were applicable in an acute setting but had poor diagnostic accuracy, and novel biomarkers were costly and of uncertain diagnostic accuracy based on limited population testing.

CRP to albumin ratio was found helpful in predicting complicated appendicitis in children. Based on a retrospective study of 296 children with acute appendicitis, a CRP/ALB ratio ≥1.39 had an 86.6% sensitivity and 84.6% specificity for complicated appendicitis with an area under the curve of 0.88.

There is greater value in combinations of findings. A CRP level >1.3 mg/dL and WBC count ≥10,000 cells/mm 3 provides strong evidence for appendicitis, as does guarding or rebound and white blood count ≥10,000 cells/mm 3 (LR+ 11.3). In the presence of <10,000 cells/mm3 and CRP level ≤1.3, appendicitis is unlikely (LR− 0.05).

Use of the APPY1 biomarker panel in adults presenting to the ED with possible acute appendicitis was also helpful in ruling out appendicitis (sensitivity of 97.5%, negative likelihood ratio of 0.07, and specificity of 36.5%). In another study, addition of APPY1 to patients with a moderate risk of appendicitis allowed reclassification of 42% to the low-risk group. APPY1 combines the values of plasma calprotectin, plasma C-reactive protein, and WBC using a mathematical algorithm and is expressed as positive or negative.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies with 8,914 patients found that a neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio >4.7 was an accurate predictor of appendicitis (89% sensitive, 91% specific) and a ratio >8.8 predicted complicated appendicitis (77% sensitive, 100% specific).

Fibrinogen may be a useful marker of acute appendicitis with a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 62% (95% CI 58%-65%) and 79% (95% CI 77%-82%), respectively. The test was more accurate in diagnosing complicated appendicitis, with a pooled sensitivity of 74% (95% CI 69%-78%), specificity of 76% (95% CI 73%-78%), and the area under the curve of 0.84.

Serum amyloid was also useful as a marker of acute appendicitis with an overall sensitivity and specificity of 87% (95% CI 79%-92%) and 74% (95% CI, 59%-85%), respectively with positive and negative likelihood ratios of 3.3 (95% CI 2.1-5.4) and 0.18 (95% CI 0.11-0.28), respectively and an area under the curve of 0.89 (95% CI 0.86-0.91).

Urinalysis may indicate UTI; however, a periappendiceal bladder inflammation may also elevate leukocyte esterase. Obtain a urine pregnancy test if the patient is of child-bearing age. Consider a chest x-ray to rule out pneumonia in younger children and infants, as the symptoms may be similar.
In one study, neither clinical findings nor laboratory tests were sufficient for determining severity of acute appendicitis.
New tests are on the horizon, including gene expression analysis of circulating WBC (riboleukogram) to rule in and/or plasma cytokines to rule out appendicitis.

Consider diagnostic imaging with computed tomography (CT) or ultrasound if symptoms are atypical or if there is a moderate likelihood of appendicitis based on Alvarado or Ohmann scores. The Surgical Infection Society and Infectious Disease Society of America recommend computed tomography (CT) as the initial diagnostic modality for adults not immediately undergoing laparotomy.

For patients with RLQ pain, fever, leukocytosis and suspected or possible appendicitis, the ACR (2022) recommends initial imaging with CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast as the preferred test. CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast, ultrasound of the abdomen or pelvis and MRI with or without contrast may be appropriate.

Authors of a systematic review of 32 studies of imaging modalities for visualizing a normal appendix found CT, ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) comparable (84%, 71% and 69%, respectively).

Interestingly, in an RCT of 185 patients with suspected appendicitis with symptoms for fewer than 24 hours and an intermediate Adult Appendicitis Score of 11-15, those randomized to immediate imaging (US followed by CT if needed) vs. observation (reassessment after 6-8 h with repeated scoring and managed accordingly) had higher rates of treatment for acute appendicitis than in the observation group (72% vs. 57%). About half (55%) of patients in the observation group did not need diagnostic imaging within 30 days after randomization and no differences in cases complicated appendicitis (4% vs. 2%, respectively) or negative appendicectomies (1% each) were observed.
CT findings include an enlarged appendix, appendicolith, pericecal inflammation, phlegmon, and abscess.

In a study comparing radiologist impression to the presence of one or more of 10 features associated with complicated appendicitis, the radiologist’s impression had a higher specificity for complicated appendicitis (76% vs. 43%) but lower sensitivity (64% vs. 92%). The 10 features are: contrast enhancement defect of the appendiceal wall, abscess, extraluminal air, intraluminal air, extraluminal appendicolith, intraluminal appendicolith, moderate-to-severe periappendiceal fat stranding, periappendiceal fluid, ileus, and ascites.
CT findings that indicate a higher risk of non-operative treatment failure (about 40%) are appendicolith, mass effect, and a dilated appendix >13 mm.

In a meta-analysis of seven studies, noncontrast CT was adequate for the diagnosis of acute appendicitis adults presenting to the emergency department (pooled estimates for sensitivity and specificity were 92.7% [95% CI, 89.5%-95.0%] and 96.1% [95% CI, 94.2%-97.5%], respectively; LR+ 24 and LR− 0.08). Similar results were found in a meta-analysis of 31 studies of CT with pooled sensitivity for CT somewhat higher at 97.2%, 95% CI 95.8 to 98.1% and pooled specificity of 95.6%, 95% CI 94.1 to 96.7%, respectively. This study included CT with contrast, which yielded the highest test characteristics.

CT is more accurate than ultrasound in detecting appendicitis in both adults and children. However, CT should be used judiciously as its safety in children has been questioned with regard to lifetime risk of radiation-induced malignancy. In addition, authors of one cohort study found that CT delayed time to operation and increased cost of care for appendicitis.

Investigators using a single-blinded RCT comparing low-dose (116 mGy·cm) with usual-dose (521 mGy·cm) CT in 891 patients with suspected appendicitis found no difference in negative appendectomy rates between groups. Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 studies confirmed non-inferiority of low-dose CT with a pooled sensitivity of 96.2% (95% CI, 91.9% to 98.3%) and specificity of 93.2% (95% CI, 88.7% to 96%).

In one retrospective study, dual-energy CT that includes virtual monoenergetic and iodine overlay imaging had high accuracy of 85.2% for confirming and excluding the presence of gangrenous appendicitis (positive predictive value 58.7% and negative predictive value 100%).

Ultrasonographic findings include a thick-walled, noncompressible appendix, which is useful to exclude ovarian pathology or ectopic pregnancy. It should be strongly considered as the initial imaging study in children and pregnant women in particular, given the absence of radiation, provided local expertise in performing the test is available.

Use of the ultrasound findings of increased appendiceal diameter, peri-appendiceal fat inflammation, presence of an appendicolith, and suspected perforation as discriminatory markers was helpful in distinguishing uncomplicated from complicated appendicitis in children.

In the meta-analysis cited above including 10 studies evaluating US and 6 evaluating both US and CT, pooled sensitivity and specificity for US was 82.1%, 95%CI 73.8 to 88.2% and 85.9%, 95%CI 72.7 to 93.3%.

In one meta-analysis, surgeon-performed bedside ultrasound had both high sensitivity and specificity for acute appendicitis. Bedside ultrasound also performed well in the hands of pediatric emergency medicine sonographers who received focused training (sensitivity of 85% [95% CI, 75%-95%], specificity of 93% [95% CI, 85%-100%], LR+ of 11.7 [95% CI, 6.9-20], and LR− of 0.17 [95% CI, 0.1-0.28]). Additional studies confirm that bedside or point-of-care ultrasound can help confirm/rule in appendicitis. The most recent review of 17 studies found a positive likelihood ratio of 9.3 in adults and 19.4 in children and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.18 in adults and 0.05 in children with point-of-care ultrasound performed by emergency physicians; however, there was significant study heterogeneity.
Sequential positioning during ultrasound examination can significantly improve appendiceal visualization and reduce the need for CT.
Combining transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound in women increased sensitivity and specificity in one study.
Based on one cost-effectiveness analysis, an ultrasound-CT protocol for appendicitis evaluation offers potentially large savings over the standard CT-only protocol, and minimizes radiation exposure.

Elastography (a measure of tissue stiffness using pre-compression correlated with post-compression images) combined with ultrasound has been suggested to increase ultrasound sensitivity. However, it is not widely used and local experience varies.

In adults with indeterminate ultrasound and clinically suspected appendicitis, a clinical decision rule can identify those at low risk of appendicitis (absence of radiation to RLQ, no vomiting, and WBC ≤12.0).

Based on a Cochrane review of 58 studies with 7,462 patients, 1,980 of whom had acute appendicitis, the sensitivity and specificity of MRI overall were 95% (95% CI 94% to 97%) and 96% (95% CI 95% to 97%), respectively, for the diagnosis of acute appendicitis. In a hypothetical cohort of 1000 patients, there would be 12 false-positive results and 30 false-negative results. For pregnant women, the sensitivity and specificity of MRI were 0.94 and 0.97 and for children both sensitivity and specificity were 0.96. Authors of this study noted that study methodological quality was poor and risk of bias was high.

An older study of both nonenhanced MRI and US demonstrated high diagnostic performance for suspected pediatric appendicitis, showing high inter-technique (κ = 0.77; 95% CI, 0.63, 0.90) and inter-observer (κ = 0.76; 95% CI, 0.61, 0.91) agreement. In a pediatric study, gadolinium-enhanced images and T2-weighted images were more helpful than non-contrast images in the assessment of acute appendicitis for patients with suspected appendicitis and indeterminate ultrasound examination.

In a prospective cohort study of 624 previously healthy children, of whom 24% had appendicitis, high clinical accuracy (134/139 [96.4%]) was demonstrated using an US-rapid-MRI pathway. MRI was used to resolve clinical vs. US discrepancies or in cases of non-diagnostic US and clinical suspicion on reassessment.

MRI was comparable to US with conditional use of CT in identifying a perforated appendix; up to half of the 31/220 patients with perforated appendicitis, however, were incorrectly classified as having simple appendicitis.

In a single institution study using tandem CT and MRI for nonpregnant patients aged 12 years and older with suspected acute appendicitis, positive and negative likelihood ratios were not significantly different at 9.4 (95% CI, 5.9, 16.4) and 0.02 (95% CI, 0.00, 0.06) for CT and 5.2 (95% CI, 3.7, 7.7) and 0.04 (95% CI, 0, 0.11) for MRI.
Use IV and rectal contrast for best delineation of abdominal structures. Oral contrast may be used instead of rectal contrast, but delays time to diagnosis and may not be tolerated by patients.

Authors of a meta-analysis of studies found that following an initial non-diagnostic US, US, CT, and MRI all had comparable and high accuracy in aiding in the diagnosis of acute appendicitis in children and adults, including pregnant women.

Although many clinical decision rules have been proposed to diagnose appendicitis, the Alvarado score (also called MANTRELS score), the Pediatric Appendicitis Score, and the Ohmann score have been best validated. Each score stratifies patients into low-, moderate-, or high-risk categories.

The newest score, RIPASA, may be superior to the Alvarado score, particularly in Asian populations. The score is more complex, and includes age, sex, nationality, signs and symptoms, elevated white blood count and negative urinalysis. Authors of a meta-analysis reporting data from 35 studies found the RIPASA score had a summary sensitivity of 0.95 (95%CI 0.92-0.97), and summary specificity of 0.71 (95%CI 0.60-0.80) compared to the Alvarado score's summary sensitivity and specificity of 0.72 (95%CI 0.66-0.77) and 0.77 (95%CI 0.70-0.82).

In a systematic review of 42 studies, authors found the Alvarado score accurate for ruling out appendicitis using a cut-point of 5 (sensitivity 99% overall) but the score over-predicted appendicitis (at a cut-point of 7), particularly in children in the intermediate- and high-risk groups and in women across all risk strata (specificity overall 81%, men 57%, woman 73%, children 76%).

Based on a systematic review, the diagnosis of appendicitis in children is ruled out with a pretest probability of acute appendicitis of 60% or less and an Alvarado score below 4 (LR- 0.02); this is also true for a score less than 5 if the pretest probability is up to approximately 40% (negative LR 0.04).

The Appendicitis Inflammatory Response (AIR) score, consisting of RLQ pain, rebound tenderness, muscular defense, WBC count, proportion of neutrophils, CRP, body temperature, and vomiting, is another score that compared favorably in one study with the Alvarado score (ROC 0.93 for appendicitis).

In a prospective before and after intervention study and nested RCT conducted in emergency departments, use of the AIR score resulted in less imaging (19.2% vs, 34.5%), fewer admissions (29.5 % vs. 42.8%), fewer negative explorations (1.6% vs. 3.2%) and fewer operations for non-perforated appendicitis (6.8% vs. 9.7%) than for the baseline period. Among patients in the intermediate-risk group, those randomized to selective imaging after clinical reassessment vs. routine imaging had the same proportion of negative appendicectomies (6.4% vs. 6.7%), number of admissions, number of perforations and length of hospital stay, but fewer patients were treated for appendicitis (46.3% vs. 53.4% in the routine imaging group).

Authors of a retrospective study of 747 consecutive children with suspected appendicitis found that the AIR had the highest discriminating power for acute appendicitis over the Alvarado and Pediatric Appendicitis Score (area under the receiver-operating curve 0.90, 0.87, and 0.82, respectively).

AIR Score: In a prospective, multicenter interventional study and nested randomized trial of Swedish adults and children with possible appendicitis, AIR scores were obtained on all patients before and after a baseline period in which scores were not shared with surgeons. Among patients scoring as low-risk (AIR score 0-4 points), the 1004 patients receiving algorithm-based observational care during the intervention period received significantly less imaging (19.2% vs. 34.5%), had fewer admissions (29.5% vs. 42.8%), and had fewer negative explorations (1.6% vs. 3.2%) and operations for non-perforated appendicitis (6·8 versus 9·7 per cent; P = 0·034) than the 586 patients from the baseline period. Among intermediate-risk patients (AIR score 5-8 points), the 543 patients randomized to immediate imaging compared to the 525 randomized to repeat AIR scoring after an observation period of 4–8 hours were more likely to be treated for appendicitis (53.4% vs. 46.3%) but had similar rates of negative appendicectomies (6.4% vs. 6.7%), number of admissions, number of perforations, and length of hospital stay.

Samuel's Pediatric Appendicitis Score: A pediatric protocol using Samuel's Pediatric Appendicitis Score (PAS) and selective use of US (performed in 128/196 patients) as the primary imaging modality, followed by CT if nondiagnostic (performed in 13/196 patients), performed well for the diagnosis of appendicitis with a negative appendectomy rate of 3/68; 4.4%).

One ED evaluated use of the following diagnostic algorithm based on the Pediatric Appendicitis Score: consult surgery if PAS >6 points, ultrasound if 4-6 points, and discharge or alternate workup if <4 points; consult surgery if the ultrasound is equivocal or indeterminate/nonvisualized, and obtain a CT scan if the surgeon is undecided. The algorithm reduced CT utilization from 75.4% to 24.2% in children with suspected appendicitis.
In a prospective study of 311 patients of whom 265 (85.2%) had acute appendicitis, neither the Alvarado score nor the PAS had adequate predictive values for assessing acute appendicitis.

Pediatric Appendicitis Score: A simple decision rule combining abdominal exam findings and WBC count is accurate in identifying children at low risk of having appendicitis. Children are at low risk if they have either an absolute neutrophil count no more than 6750/microliter and no RLQ tenderness OR an absolute neutrophil count no more than 6750/microliter with maximal tenderness in the RLQ but no abdominal pain with walking, jumping, or coughing.

Use of an 11-node decision tree for 244 adult patients with equivocal CT findings for acute appendicitis outperformed the Alvarado and Eskelinen scores in one retrospective study; confidence intervals overlapped for the adult appendicitis scores.

The Adult Appendicitis Score including aspects of RLQ pain and laboratory findings for blood leukocyte count, proportion of neutrophils and CRP performed better at ruling out appendicitis than the Alvarado score in a retrospective study including 1303 cases of acute appendicitis.

The Pediatric Appendicitis Laboratory Score (PALabS), a score that combines clinical features and laboratory values, was also accurate in ruling out acute appendicitis in children. 220710 PALabS consists of 6 parts: nausea (3 points), maximal pain in the RLQ (4 points), absolute neutrophil count above 7500 per microliter (7 points), white blood cell count above 10,000 per microliter (4 points), C-reactive protein above 10 mg per liter (2 points), and calprotectin above 50 nanograms per milliliter (3 points). In the derivation group, the PALabS was accurate with an area under the curve of 0.88 and in the validation cohort, a PALabS of 6 or less was 99.2% sensitive (95% CI, 95.6 - 99.9) and had a negative likelihood ratio of 0.03 (0.00 - 0.18). Specificity was about 32%.

A clinical decision rule based on the presence of fewer than two of the following predictors: male sex, migration of pain to the RLQ, vomiting, and WBC count >12.0 × 109/L significantly reduced the probability of appendicitis in a large subgroup of patients with negative or inconclusive US results. The addition of CRP results did not improve prediction.

The pediatric Appendicitis Risk Calculator (pARC) outperformed the PAS in a study of 2,089 children presenting to the emergency department with a chief complaint of abdominal pain and less than or equal to 5 days of right-sided or diffuse abdominal pain. Appendicitis was confirmed in 16.9%. The area under the curve was significantly higher for the pARC at 0.89 compared to 0.8 for the PAS. The calculator uses setting; gender; pain duration; WBC; % neutrophils; and presence or absence of pain when walking, maximal tenderness in RLQ, guarding, and migration of pain to the RLQ.

In a study of 475 patients, one guideline recommended immediate surgery for those with WBC >10,000, >67% PMNs, guarding and or focal RLQ tenderness, and >13 hours abdominal pain. Discharge with 12-hour follow-up was recommended for those with none of those findings, and observation/imaging for the remainder. They had a 2% missed appendicitis rate and 1% negative appendectomy rate.

In one study, complicated appendicitis was predicted using abdominal pain severity, temperature, WBC and CRP for a total score of 7 which had an area under the curve of 0.857. In this study, 1 point was given when the abdominal pain range was >3, the highest body temperature was >37.9°C, peripheral blood WBC was >13.66 109/L, and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio was >10.9, and 3 points were given when CRP was >66.1 mg/L.

A negative Heidelberg Appendicitis Score appears useful in ruling out perforated appendicitis in children (negative predictive value 100%). This score is positive 0 with 3 or more of the following features: continuous abdominal pain, tenderness on the right lower quadrant, rebound tenderness and conspicuous ultrasound.

Consider using the Alvarado, Pediatric Appendicitis Score (PAS), Ohmann, or RIPASA score to stratify patients into low-, moderate-, or high-risk categories. An experienced surgeon's judgment is similarly accurate.

See for a suggested approach to management. A study of a protocol that incorporated risk assessment, initial ultrasound, and selective use of CT found that 37% of patients coud go to the OR without any imaging, 58% were managed without a CT, and the rates of missed appendicitis and negative appendectomy were 2% and 1% respectively.

Routine use of CT is not recommended, as it increases cost, may delay definitive therapy, and is associated with a similar negative appendectomy rate (6%-10%) to that of an experienced surgeon. In one study of children with suspected appendicitis, high adherence to use of a clinical pathway with ultrasound as the initial imaging modality reduced use of CT from 94.2% (130/138) to 27.5% (78/284) and had a negative appendectomy rate of 2.4%.

Treatment of pain does not negatively influence outcome in suspected appendicitis. In a RCT of 213 patients, negative appendectomy rates were similar in the saline placebo group vs. morphine group (3.8% vs. 3.2%) as were perforation rates (18.9% in the placebo group vs. 14.3% in the morphine pain control group).
Early surgical consult is imperative. Initial management consists of no food or drink, intravenous fluids, and antibiotics. A
Adequate analgesia is essential. B

Appendectomy is the standard treatment. A Antibiotics or observation/supportive care alone and reassessment can be considered for primary treatment for patients presenting with suspected uncomplicated appendicitis. B
For patients with complicated appendicitis, including pregnant patients, operative management is likely preferred over non-operative management. B
For ruptured appendicitis, nonoperative management may be considered under surgeon guidance. A
Initially, the patient is kept from eating or drinking and given intravenous fluids and antibiotics that cover enteric flora.

Antibiotics are recommended to prevent postoperative complications. Antibiotics should be initiated prior to surgery and continued postoperatively for 24 hours if the appendix is not perforated. For perforated appendicitis, antibiotics should be continued for 7 days with either an intravenous or oral regimen.

In an open-label, non-inferiority trial of 1066 patients over age 7 years with complicated appendicitis undergoing primarily (95%) laparoscopic appendectomy in 15 hospitals in the Netherlands, 2 days of postoperative intravenous antibiotics was non-inferior to 5 days with respect to infectious complications and mortality within 90 days. Although the rate of re-interventions was similar between trial groups, fewer patients had antibiotic adverse effects in the 2-day group (9% vs. 22% in the 5-day group), but re-admission to hospital was more frequent in the 2-day group (12% vs. 6%).

Regimens that minimize dosing frequency are most effective. Two suggested regimens are piperacillin/tazobactam and ceftriaxone and metronidazole. Single-agent antibiotic therapy is equal in efficacy to the traditional aminoglycoside-based combination therapy and may offer improvements in terms of length of stay, pharmacy charges, and hospital charges. Additional antibiotic recommendations, based on local resistance patterns can be found in the guideline by the Surgical Infection Society and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

A single-blind RCT of 1,774 patients with uncomplicated appendicitis compared immediate preoperative antibiotics (IV cefuroxime 1,500 mg plus metronidazole 500 mg every 8 hours) with no antibiotics while patients awaited surgery scheduled within 8 to 24 hours. All patients also received one dose of the same regimen at anesthesia induction. The trial found that starting antibiotics immediately after diagnosis did not reduce the risk of appendiceal perforation in adults when surgery was performed within 24 hours. Among the secondary outcomes, however, the risk of surgical site infection was slightly lower with immediate preoperative antibiotics (NNT = 63; 95% CI, 32–641).

Nonoperative management usually involves antibiotics. In optimal circumstances, the appendix does not require resection. Nonoperative management may result in a lower complication rate and a shorter hospital stay, and likely reduces costs. Common regimens are IV ceftriaxone, cefoxitin or ertapenem for 24 hours followed by 5–10 days of ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin plus metronidazole.

In two meta-analyses of RCTs of antibiotic therapy vs. surgery for acute appendicitis, however, there were no significant differences in hospital stay or complication rates between groups; of the patients randomized to the antibiotic group. Most (68% and 63%, respectively in the two studies) were successfully treated, 32% and 21%, respectively, crossed over to the surgery group, and 15% and 20%, respectively, were readmitted.

In one RCT, 72.7% of the 256 patients randomized to antibiotics did not require appendectomy. Those who underwent appendectomy within one year after initial antibiotic treatment experienced fewer postsurgical complications than the group of patients who underwent immediate appendectomy. In a 5-year follow-up of patients enrolled in this trial, investigators found a cumulative incidence of acute appendicitis recurrence in the antibiotic group of 39.5% (95% CI, 33.1% - 45.3%). Among patients requiring subsequent appendectomy, no additional adverse outcomes were related to the delay.

In the largest and most recent RCT of 1552 patients randomized to surgery or intravenous antibiotic antibiotics for at least 24 hours followed by an oral antibiotic for a 10-day total course, short-term quality of life was similar between groups but patients in the antibiotic group had more emergency department visits (9% vs 4%) and more hospitalizations (24% vs 5%) following treatment, and 30% required appendectomy within 90 days of index treatment. Patients with appendicoliths, compared to those without appendicoliths, were more likely to require appendectomy at 90 days (41% vs 25%) and had a higher rate of complications (20.2 vs 3.6 per 100 participants), and might be considered more appropriate for surgery.

In a secondary analysis of data from this trial (CODA), of the 776 patients randomized to antibiotics, 42 (5.4%) underwent appendectomy within 24 hours, 335 (46.1%) were discharged within 24 hours, and serious adverse events occurred over 7 days in 0.9 (95% CI 0.2-2.6) per 100 outpatients and 1.3 (95% CI 0.4-2.9) per 100 inpatients.

In the most recent meta-analysis of 12 RCTs of patients with uncomplicated acute appendicitis, complication-free treatment success was significantly lower for non-operative therapy vs. surgery at 1-year follow-up (69.4% vs. 88.8%; RR 0.81; 95% CI 0.73-0.91). Post-treatment surgical complication rates, negative appendectomy rates, length of hospital stay, and quality of life at 1 month were similar in the antibiotic and surgery groups.

The ten-year observational follow-up of patients in the Appendicitis Acuta (APPAC) multicenter RCT found that in patients originally randomized to antibiotics the appendicitis recurrence rate was 37.8% (95% CI, 31.6%-44.1%) and the cumulative appendectomy rate was 44.3% (95% CI, 38.2%-50.4%). The authors conclude that antibiotics should be considered an option for uncomplicated acute appendicitis in adults.

Interestingly, in a British RCT of 245 patients with uncomplicated appendicitis, total treatment failure rates were similar between patients randomized to a no-antibiotic regimen with supportive care (intravenous fluids, analgesia and antipyretics as necessary) or a 4-day course of antibiotics with supportive care (20.7% vs. 23.4%, respectively). Of the 18 patients experiencing initial treatment failure, 15 underwent appendectomy and 3 received additional antibiotics. Recurrence occurred in 20 patients in the no-antibiotic group and 16 patients in the antibiotic group, of whom 30 underwent appendicectomy and 6 received antibiotics.

In an RCT of 66 adults with CT-confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis, placebo treatment was noninferior to antibiotics (intravenous ertapenem followed by oral levofloxacin and metronidazole), with a 10-day treatment success rate of 87% (95% CI 75-99%) and 97% (95% CI 92-100%), respectively.

Pain control is important. Opiates generally do not interfere with diagnosis or management. Narcotics and acetaminophen are the mainstay for analgesia and antipyresis. Intravenous ketorolac is often added postoperatively.

In one RCT of open appendectomy, patients randomized to local bupivacaine infiltrated both subcutaneously (SC) and deep-to the external oblique prior to incision to create a local nerve field blockade used less postoperative analgesia (60% vs. 100% for the SC only and placebo injection groups) and had delayed time to first analgesic requirement).

Use of pulsed electromagnetic field for postoperative pain management was not superior to sham device use following appendectomy based on an RCT of 118 adult patients with acute appendicitis. In another RCT, magnetic acupuncture in children undergoing laparoscopic appendectomy reduced postoperative pain perception and on-demand use of analgesics.
Use of intraperitoneal local anesthetic did not result in lower pain scores in children undergoing laparoscopic appendectomy.
An early surgical consult is imperative.

A short delay of up to 24 hours before appendectomy is not associated with increased rates of complex pathology (perforation, gangrene, and/or abscess) in adults or children with acute appendicitis. After 48 hours, the risk of surgical site infection and 30-day adverse events appear to increase.
Better cosmetic results were reported in one RCT using continuous absorbable intradermal suturing compared to interrupted nonabsorbable sutures for open appendectomy.

Performing peritoneal lavage during appendectomy has no advantage over suction or drainage with respect to intra-abdominal abscess or surgical-site infection based on a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs with 1487 patients.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 75 trials with 8520 adults and 10 trials with 1245 children concluded that laparoscopic surgery had advantages over open surgery of lower pain intensity on day one, fewer wound infections, and reduced length of hospital stay and time until return to normal activity in adults and reduced wound infections and length of hospital stay in children.
Although the incidence of wound infection is lower after laparoscopic appendectomy, there may be a higher incidence of intraabdominal abscess.

In addition to the above findings, authors of a meta-analysis found laparoscopic appendectomy was associated with earlier resumption of food, a reduction in doses of parenteral and oral analgesics, better cosmesis, and similar hospital charges. Operative time was about 13 minutes longer with laparoscopic vs. open surgery.

Similar results were found for laparoscopic versus open appendectomy for complicated appendicitis in a retrospective analysis of cases. No differences, however, were found in intra-operative duration, rate of wound sepsis, number of re-operations, length of hospital stay or rate of re-admissions between open and laparoscopic appendectomy for complicated appendicitis in a RCT of 114 patients.

In a database study of obese patients, laparoscopic appendectomy, performed in 78% of cases, vs. open appendectomy was associated with similar mortality but a 57% reduction in overall morbidity after attempting to account for preoperative risk factors.

Authors of a Cochrane review,found usee of laparoscopy versus open appendectomy in women of childbearing age with acute lower abdominal pain resulted in an increased rate of specific diagnoses (OR 4.10; 95% CI 2.50-6.71) but no difference in rates of adverse events; similar results were shown for laparoscopy versus a “wait-and-see” approach. A meta-analysis of 7 of the studies found a significant difference favoring laparoscopy in the rate of removal of a normal appendix (OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.24).

Outpatient laparoscopic appendectomy is offered by some centers. In one cohort of 345 patients with apparently uncomplicated appendicitis, the success rate was 88%. Forty patients (12%) were admitted for preexisting comorbidities, postoperative morbidity (6 patients), or lack of transportation or home support. There were no deaths and 6.6% experienced postoperative morbidity. Four patients (1%) were readmitted for transient fever, nausea/vomiting, partial small bowel obstruction, and deep venous thrombosis.

In an RCT of 97 patients admitted from the emergency department with uncomplicated acute appendicitis, there was no difference in readmission rate, further emergency consultations or complications between inpatient and outpatient laparoscopy. The cost saving was $516.52/patient for those receiving care in the day-surgery unit.

Authors of four meta-analyses found similar 30-day postoperative morbidity and wound infection rates for single-incision vs. conventional laparoscopic appendectomy, although mean operative times were longer by about 6-8 minutes with the single-incision procedure. Single port procedures may offer better cosmesis.
Single-port laparoscopic appendectomy has been used successfully in children (case series).

Early post-operative pain at 1-4 hours was less with single-dermatome laparoscopic appendectomy (all trocars are placed at the same dermatome field) than standard laparoscopy in one RCT, but there was no difference at 6 or more hours post-operatively.
Use of a specimen-retrieval bag did not reduce surgical site infection in patients undergoing laparoscopic appendectomy in one RCT.
If there is perforation with abscess or phlegmon formation, nonoperative management may be considered. The decision for nonoperative treatment is based on multiple factors.
Percutaneous drainage of the fluid collection may hasten symptom resolution.

In two small RCTs of patients with perforated appendix, delayed primary closure at day 4 to 5 or longer postoperatively led to decreased subsequent wound infection than primary closure (2.9% vs. 38.9% in one trial and 6.3% vs. 39.2% in the other) and decreased length of stay (6.3 vs. 8.4 days in the first cited trial).

Randomization to use of intraoperative strong acid electrolyzed water vs. saline for peritoneal lavage and washing out the wound reduced postoperative surgical site infection (0 vs. 20%) but did not prevent residual abscess (1 case in each group) in 44 children with perforated appendix.

Endoscopic retrograde appendicitis therapy consists of passage of a colonoscope to the opening of the appendix for placement of a stent or drain in the infected appendix via the appendiceal orifice, relieving appendiceal obstruction. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 primarily single-center studies including 298 patients with appendicitis found a pooled rate of clinical success of 99.29 % (95 % CI 97.48 % to 100 %; I 2 = 0 %) and appendiceal perforation occurred in 3 patients. Average procedure length was 41.1 ± 7.16 minutes with an average hospital length of stay of 3.93 ± 1.01 days. Recurrence occurred in 22 patients (7.4%). The authors note that the studies occurred in single centers with advanced endoscopists and findings may not be generalizable.
Treatment duration is directed by intraoperative findings.

In nonperforated appendicitis, inpatients are typically discharged after 24 hours if they tolerate a diet and have adequate analgesia. They may receive 24 hours of intravenous antibiotics, although the routine use of antibiotics is unnecessary. Same day discharge of children with uncomplicated appendicitis following appendectomy may be appropriate.

In perforated appendicitis, patients may develop a significant ileus. Wait for the return of bowel function before starting a diet. In prolonged cases, total parenteral nutrition may be considered. Antibiotics should be continued until the patient is afebrile for 24 hours, tolerates food, and has a normal WBC count.

In one RCT of 518 patients with complicated intra-abdominal infection, there were no differences in outcomes between providing antibiotics until 2 days after resolution of fever, leukocytosis, and ileus (median duration 8 days) vs. a fixed duration of 4 days. The rate of the primary outcome—a composite of surgical-site infection, recurrent intra-abdominal infection, or death within 30 days—was high for both groups at 22.3% and 21.8%, respectively.
Delay in treatment can result in complications. Late presentation is more likely to be associated with appendix rupture and, therefore, wound infection and abdominal abscess formation.
If appropriate resources are not available for potentially complex pediatric cases, or if the child is younger than 8 years, they should be directly transferred to an appropriate center.
In elderly patients with significant comorbidities, consideration may be given to transfer to a tertiary care center for management of potential postoperative complications.
In low-risk patients, observation is warranted if the patient and family are aware of the progressive symptoms that may be indicative of appendicitis.

The overall complication rate is 3%, but the complication rate increases with perforation. In one study using the National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database, blacks were more likely than whites to suffer serious postoperative complications (4.8% vs. 3.3%; adjusted odds ratio [OR] 1.39; 95% CI, 1.16-1.67) or any complication (8.4% vs. 6.0%; adjusted OR 1.31; 95% CI, 1.14-1.50).

The most common complication is local wound infection in 3% to 11%, which is treated with local care and antibiotics. Deeper soft-tissue infections are rare in children and are treated with wet to dry dressings.
Intraabdominal abscesses occur in 0.08% to 2% of patients and are treated with antibiotics and percutaneous drainage.

Appendicitis in the residual stump following surgery is rare; in one literature review of 62 cases, including 2 cases at the authors’ institution, stump appendicits occurred following both open and laparoscopic procedures at an interval of 4 days to 50 years. CT was diagnostic in just under half the cases and 40% had gangrene and had perforated.

In a retrospective chart review from two university hospitals, one using mostly open appendectomy and the other laparoscopic appendectomy for suspected acute appendicitis, rates of readmission for small bowel obstruction were low but higher for those treated with open procedures (1.0% in the open group vs. 0.4% in the laparoscopic group).

In one retrospective study, appendiceal tumor was found in 2.5% of 677 consecutive adult patients who underwent appendectomy over 4 years. Risk factors included age ≥50 years (OR 3.6; 95% CI, 1.1-11.4), outpatient steroid/immunosuppressant use (OR 12.1; 95% CI, 2.0-72.5), absence of migratory RLQ pain (OR 4.7; 95% CI, 1.2-18.1), and the appearance of a phlegmon on CT scan (OR 7.0; 95% CI, 1.6-30.2); area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.86 (95% CI, 0.71-0.97].

Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 retrospective studies and one RCT of interval appendectomy in patients with complicated appendicitis found a higher pooled prevalence of neoplasms of 11% (95% CI 7-15; I2 = 37.5%). These included appendiceal mucinous neoplasms in 43%, adenocarcinoma in 29%, appendiceal neuroendocrine neoplasm in 21%, goblet cell carcinoma in 13%, and adenoma or serrated lesions in 20% of cases.

Nasogastric suction may relieve postoperative nausea and vomiting. Small bowel obstruction may respond to nasogastric decompression but may require operative intervention. However, routine use of nasogastric suctioning after abdominal surgery was not found to be of benefit, and patients without suctioning had earlier return of bowel function.
Chewing gum reduces postoperative ileus after open appendectomy.
Ranitidine or diphenhydramine given to patients with perforated appendicitis may increase the risk of postoperative abscess.
The natural history of appendicitis is perforation, and if not treated, may lead to sepsis and shock.
Once treatment is initiated, prognosis is excellent.
There appears to be a racial disparity, however, with blacks experiencing more serious postoperative complications (4.8% vs. 3.3%) or any complication (8.4% vs. 6.0%).
Other than a postoperative visit, there is no need for follow-up, except for those electing nonoperative management.

Among adults over age 40 years, there is some concern about colonic neoplasms as a potential causative factor. In a retrospective study of 731 post-appendectomy, colonic neoplasms were found in 7.4% including 9 colorectal cancers, 7 of which were right-sided. Colonoscopy was performed in 43.2% within 3 years after admission. Follow-up CT scan, however, had high specificity of 97% but low sensitivity of 25%.
Older patients have higher rate of perforation, likely due to age-related changes of the appendix, delay in seeking care, nonspecific symptoms, and atypical presentations.

Appendicitis is the most common nonobstetric surgical diagnosis in pregnancy. Physical examination on presentation is the most reliable diagnostic tool. There is a higher incidence of perforation with increased gestational age, but it does not result in increased fetal mortality.

There is a slightly higher incidence of appendicitis in the second trimester. An enlarged uterus displaces the appendix, resulting in atypical symptoms. However, RLQ tenderness is still the most common presenting symptom.
Because of a delay in diagnosis, there is a higher rate of perforation.

In a study of 164 pregnant women undergoing MRI for suspected acute appendicitis, of whom 28 (17%) had confirmed appendicitis, a left shift with neutrophils >70% had a sensitivity and negative predictive value for appendicitis of 100%.
ACR (2022) recommends unenhanced MRI and ultrasound as the diagnostic procedures of choice in pregnant patients.

Ultrasound for diagnosis of acute appendicitis has low diagnostic accuracy with a recent meta-analysis showing sensitivities in the first, second, and third trimesters of pregnancy of 69%, 63%, and 51%, respectively and specificities of 85%, 85%, and 65%. MRI can be useful in pregnant women with suspected appendicitis when ultrasound is inconclusive; its high negative predictive value may decrease the need for emergency surgery. In one study, use of MRI for suspected appendicitis in pregnant women reduced length of stay and increased discharges from the emergency department.

In a case series of 4-day antibiotic treatment of uncomplicated acute appendicitis in 20 pregnant women, only 3 required initial appendectomy and 2 more women received a new course of antibiotics during pregnancy at 3- and 6-months post-treatment. Two women experienced recurrence at 8- and 10-months post-treatment and underwent appendectomy.
Authors of a meta-analysis found that laparoscopic appendectomy in pregnant women was associated with a greater risk of fetal loss; quality of evidence was low.

European Association of Endoscopic Surgery (EAES) recommends operative treatment over conservative management in pregnant patients with complicated appendicitis or appendicolith on imaging studies. For patients with acute appendicitis prior to 20 weeks gestation, or when the fundus of the uterus is below the level of the umbilicus, EAES suggests performing laparoscopic surgery and either laparoscopic or open surgery after 20 weeks or with a uterus above the umbilicus.

Abdominal pain in children is often misdiagnosed, and the diagnosis of appendicitis is typically made in a toddler after perforation. This is because of nonspecific symptoms, poor communication, and a thinner muscularis layer of the appendix.

Diagnosis Authors of a systematic review found that the Pediatric Appendicitis Score outpredicted the Alvarado Score but that neither met performance benchmarks for predicting acute appendicitis in children. In another study, children with inconclusive focused appendicitis ultrasound findings and an Alvarado score of <5 were extremely unlikely to have appendicitis (negative predictive value 99.6%).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 67 studies including 34,839 children of whom 13,342 had appendicitis, found the best performing single blood tests for ruling-out appendicitis are a white blood cell count <10 000 cells/µ or absolute neutrophil count <7500 cells/µL; a combination of white cell count and CRP further increased sensitivity. In a hypothetical cohort of 1000 children with appendicitis symptoms, 400 would have appendicitis, 60 and 40 children would be wrongly discharged based solely on WCC and ANC, respectively, and 12 using a combination of WCC and CRP. The most specific tests for ruling in appendicitis were CRP alone (≥50 mg/L; 38 studies; specificity 0.87, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.91) or combined CRP with WCC ≥10 000 cells/µL (6 studies; sensitivity 0.93, 95% CI 0.91 to 0.95).

Investigators using a Classification and Regression Tree analysis identified a classification algorithm based on the Pediatric appendicitis score, neutrophils percentage and CRP that predicted complicated appendicitis better than other combinations of the outcome parameters with a 90% sensitivity and 78.6% specificity.

Imaging ACR (2018) recommends no initial imaging in a child with suspected acute appendicitis at low clinical risk. In a child with suspected acute appendicitis at intermediate clinical risk, abdominal ultrasound was recommended as usually appropriate with CT or MRI without or with contrast as possibly appropriate. For those at high clinical risk, imaging that may be appropriate included abdominal RLQ ultrasound, CT with contrast, or MRI without contrast.

When abdominal ultrasound is nondiagnostic, either CT with contrast or MRI without or with contrast were usually deemed appropriate by ACR. CT was preferred over MRI in cases with suspected acute appendicitis with clinical suspicion or initial imaging suggestive of a complication (e.g., abscess, bowel obstruction).
Low-dose CT was comparable to standard CT for final diagnosis of acute appendicitis following equivocal results based on an RCT of 3074 patients aged 15-44 years.

In children with suspected appendicitis, authors of a study of 104 consecutive children found that diagnostic strategies using MRI only or conditional MRI had a higher sensitivity for appendicitis compared with ultrasound only. In another study, staged US and unenhanced MRI was 98.2% sensitive and 97.1% specific for the diagnosis of appendicitis in children.

Non-operative management Less in known about the safety of initial antibiotic treatment for acute appendicitis in children. In an RCT of 50 children with imaging-confirmed nonperforated acute appendicitis, twenty-two of 24 patients (92%) treated with antibiotics had initial resolution and 1 patient had recurrence of acute appendicitis at 9 months; there were no serious complications in the operative group. Another 6 children had an appendectomy due to recurrent abdominal pain (n = 5) or parental wish (n = 1) during the follow-up period; none had histopathological evidence of appendicitis.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 studies with 404 patients found non-operative management initially successful in 152/168 children (90.5%), but 45 of the antibiotic-treated children (26.8%) underwent appendectomy within the following year. Treatment failure was increased in patients with an appendicolith.

In a second meta-analysis of 10 studies including 6 observational studies and a single RCT, non-operative treatment was initially successful in 97% of children (95% CI, 96%-99%) and remained successful in 82% of children (95% CI, 77%-87%) at 8 weeks to 4 years of follow-up. Recurrent appendicitis was reported in 14% (95% CI, 7%-21%).

In another meta-analysis of 4 cohort studies and 1 RCT of appendicectomy and non-operative management of acute uncomplicated appendicitis in children, authors reported reduced treatment efficacy of the nonoperative approach (RR 0.77; 95% CI, 0.71-0.84) with an increased readmission rate (RR 6.98; 95% CI, 2.07-23.6). The complication rate for the two approaches was comparable.

In a 2025 unblinded RCT researchers randomized children (5–16 years of age) with clinically suspected acute nonperforated appendicitis to receive intravenous antibiotics (n = 477) or laparoscopic appendectomy (n = 459). The primary outcome was treatment failure within twelve months, defined as the need for surgery in the antibiotics-treated children and appendicitis-related complications or negative findings at the time of surgery in the surgery-treated children. ATreatment failure occurred in 34% children treated with antibiotics vs. 7% in those treated with surgery (number needed to treat = 4).

Other relevant outcomes to consider were evaluated in a feasibility randomized trial. Of 26 children for whom data were available, children allocated to non-operative treatment vs. appendectomy reported higher short-term quality of life scores, shorter duration of requiring analgesia, more rapid return to normal activities and shorter parental absence from work.

Among 370 patients (34.6% of 1068 total patients) enrolled in a nonoperative group, treatment failure occurred for 125 patients (33.8%) at 1 year. There were no differences in treatment failures based on demographic factors, symptoms at presentation, or imaging results. Higher patient-reported pain at presentation was associated with increased risk of in-hospital treatment failure (RR 2.1, 95% CI 1.0-4.4) but not delayed or overall treatment failure.

A meta-analysis of seven RCTs involving 1,480 pediatric patients comparing nonoperative management (NOM) with appendectomy found that, at 1 year, treatment failure and major complications were significantly more common with NOM (RR 4.97 and 33.37, respectively). NOM was also associated with a faster return to school and normal activities, although the authors noted that these benefits may be offset by the aforementioned harms.
Surgical management Authors of a large database study of over 250,000 appendectomies in children found a negative appendectomy rate of 6.7%.

For children with uncomplicated acute appendicitis, authors of a systematic review of 73,150 cases found that laparoscopic appendectomy vs. open surgery was associated with a reduced hospital stay but equivalent postoperative morbidity. For the 34,474 children with complicated appendicitis, the laparoscopic approach was associated with reduced overall complications, wound infections, length of hospital stay, and bowel obstruction episodes but increased risk of intra-abdominal abscess.

For complicated appendicitis, authors of a recent meta-analysis of 4 RCTs and 36 case-controlled studies found that laparoscopic appendectomy had advantages compared to open surgery with a shorter length of stay, a lower rate of surgical site infection, and a significantly lower overall complication rate. Rates of intraabdominal abscess formation, post-operative fever, pneumonia and ileus were similar between groups.

If one assumes clinical equipoise between open and laparoscopic procedures in children, especially with uncomplicated appendicitis, cost considerations favor the open procedure. In one study, after providing cost information through videos (about $1500 less), more patients and parents chose the open procedure.

Perforated appendix Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 studies with 1633 children with perforated appendix found no significant difference in the incidence of postoperative intraabdominal abscess, wound infection, or length of hospitalization between peritoneal irrigation and suction alone, but duration of surgery was longer in irrigation group.

In a pilot study of 100 children with perforated appendix, irrigation with povidone-iodine resulted in similar occurrences of postoperative intra-abdominal abscess compared to no irrigation (12% vs. 16%, respectively) but fewer ED visits and readmissions, and shorter initial and total 30-day length of stay.

Based on 16 studies including 5108 children with complicated appendicitis, prophylactic drain placement following appendectomy significantly increased risk of intra-peritoneal abscess formation, but there was no difference in rates of wound infection. Length of stay was significantly longer by a mean of 2 days in the drain group.

In one RCT of children following laparoscopic surgery for perforated appendix, discharge to home on oral amoxicillin/clavulanate to complete 7 days treatment versus IV antibiotics for a minimum of 5 days was equally effective, with no difference in postoperative abscess formation.

cell.label: Assess risk for appendicitis
cell.path: Low risk (<5% appendicitis): Alvarado score <4 points or Ohmann score <6 points
High risk: Alvarado score >7 points, Ohmann score ≥12 points, or WBC count ≥10,000 cells per mm3 (10 × 109 per L) plus CRP level >1.3 mg per dL (12 mg per L) or guarding/rebound tenderness

footnotes.footnote: NOTE: At any time, clinical judgment may supersede recommendation for imaging or intervention.
*This algorithm is based on studies that were largely limited to adults and children 6 years and older.
WBC, white blood cell count; CRP, C-reactive protein; CT, computed tomography.
